summary:
We built SPHEREx SkyBlink to make real infrared astronomy data easier to explore. It is a browser-based workspace where people can enter sky coordinates or choose one of five featured targets, then compare NASA SPHEREx observations taken at different times. Users can step through images, blink between them, view them side by side, and inspect difference images when available. They can also explore spectral samples and see the dates, sources, warnings, and evidence behind each result. We wanted the experience to feel approachable for students, educators, citizen scientists, and researchers, while still being honest about what the data can actually show.
Our Python backend retrieves scientific FITS files, removes supported background signals, handles flagged pixels, aligns observations, and checks wavelength compatibility before comparing them. We built the interface with React and TypeScript, used FastAPI and scientific Python libraries for processing, and connected to NASA/IPAC IRSA for data. Because archive search is currently affected by upstream failures, we added clear options for known exposure lists and saved examples made from real observations. SkyBlink also supports shareable views, downloadable measurements, keyboard controls, and reduced motion. We want people to spot interesting patterns, ask questions, and understand when a finding needs more evidence.
details:
We built **SPHEREx SkyBlink** to make it easier to explore how the infrared sky changes over time. You can enter sky coordinates or pick one of five featured targets, then compare real NASA SPHEREx observations by stepping through images, blinking between them, viewing them side by side, or looking at difference images when available. We also brought spectral samples, observation dates, data sources, and supporting evidence into the same workspace. We wanted people to be able to spot interesting changes without having to write code or manage large scientific files, while still seeing when the data is incomplete or a result is uncertain. SkyBlink is a tool for asking better questions, not for automatically confirming a discovery.

Behind the scenes, we built a Python backend that retrieves and processes scientific FITS files, handles background signals and flagged pixels, lines observations up, and checks whether they can fairly be compared. We used FastAPI and scientific libraries including Astropy, NumPy, and SciPy, with a React and TypeScript frontend. The data comes from NASA/IPAC IRSA, and we used GitHub, pytest, and browser checks during development. Archive search is currently affected by upstream failures, so we added clear options to use known exposure lists or saved examples from real observations.
